abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a paradigm-shifting theoretical framework for analyzing nonlinear circuits based onkoopman operator theory combined with machine learning-derived basis functions. Traditional approaches to nonlinear circuit analysis rely on perturbation methods or harmonic balance techniques, which struggle with strongly nonlinear behavior and high-dimensional systems. The proposed methodology maps the nonlinear circuit dynamics onto an infinite-dimensional linear space where the Koopman operator governs the evolution, enabling linear analysis techniques to be applied to inherently nonlinear problems. We demonstrate that by learning Koopman observables from circuit simulation data, we can predict transient responses, steady-state behavior, and stability boundaries with orders of magnitude improvement in computational efficiency compared to conventional methods. The framework provides rigorous guarantees on approximation accuracy through spectral analysis of the estimated operator. Application examples include switched-capacitor circuits, oscillators with nonlinear phase noise, and power converter feedback systems, where the method captures bifurcations and limit cycles that traditional linearization misses. This work establishes a new paradigm connecting dynamical systems theory to practical circuit design, opening avenues for automated analysis and optimization of complex mixed-signal systems.

This paper presents a significantly improved harmonic balance (HB) methodology for efficient analysis of RF and microwave circuits with strong nonlinearities. Conventional HB suffers from exponential complexity growth with the number of harmonics and requires careful handling of frequency translation in feedback loops. The proposed approach introduces a hierarchical shooting method combined with adaptive harmonic selection, reducing computational complexity from O(N^h) to O(N log N) where N is the circuit size and h is the harmonic count. We derive new convergence criteria based on energy conservation principles that ensure solution accuracy while enabling aggressive pruning of insignificant harmonic terms. The methodology incorporates intelligent initialization using envelope transient results to guarantee convergence for difficult cases such as oscillators and frequency dividers. Experimental validation on a 28 GHz CMOS power amplifier demonstrates a 15x speedup over commercial HB solvers while maintaining accuracy within 0.5 dB for fundamental and harmonic power predictions. The approach extends naturally to mixed-signal circuits with clocked elements, providing designers with an efficient tool for large-signal RF circuit simulation.

This paper presents a fundamentally new architecture for high-speed analog-to-digital conversion based on time-mode signal processing rather than traditional voltage-mode sampling. The proposed time-domain ADC exploits the inherent advantages of digital CMOS technology by converting input voltages to time delays using voltage-controlled delay lines, then measuring these delays with a fully digital time-to-digital converter. This paradigm shift eliminates the need for high-gain analog amplifiers and precision analog components, achievingadc performance primarily through digital circuit scaling. A prototype 10-bit 2 GS/s ADC implemented in 28 nm CMOS demonstrates effective resolution bandwidth of 1.2 GHz while consuming only 1.8 mW from a 0.9 V supply. The architecture enables native digital background calibration with minimal hardware overhead, achieving INL/DNL below 0.3 LSB without analog trimming. The time-mode approach exhibits inherent anti-aliasing properties and relaxed settling requirements compared to switched-capacitor architectures. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the proposed topology scales favorably with technology nodes, offering a compelling path for future ultra-high-speed data converters in communications and instrumentation applications.

This paper presents a power-optimized successive approximation register (SAR) analog-to-digital converter with innovative techniques achieving significant improvements in energy efficiency for biomedical sensor interfaces. The design addresses the fundamental trade-off between conversion speed and power consumption through three key innovations: a split-capacitor DAC with unit-element redundancy that relaxes comparator noise requirements by 6 dB, a dual-path asynchronous logic architecture that reduces switching activity by 40%, and a dynamic biasing scheme that adapts power consumption to input signal statistics. The 12-bit 1 MS/s ADC occupies 0.15 mm^2 in 180 nm CMOS and achieves 92.5 dB SNDR while consuming only 4.5 µW, representing a 3x improvement in figure-of-merit compared to prior art. A novel reference buffer design using composite cascoded structures achieves reference current independence, eliminating the need for off-chip decoupling capacitors. The converter includes an integrated digital decimation filter optimized for neural recording applications, providing 60 dB stopband attenuation. Measurement results across corner lots confirm robust performance, and the design methodology is generalizable to other low-power sensor interface applications requiring high dynamic range in compact form factors.
